title: What are you doing?
goal: Recognize all four verb groups from their dictionary form and use them all in the present tense, including mixed verbs like facio.
bekal: guess a verb's group just from its second form
build the six forms of *video*, *mitto* and *audio* without looking at a table
read Latin sentences containing verbs from all four groups at once

dialogs.title: Colloquium — In schola, hora tertia
dialogs.intro: Third lesson of the day. Everyone is busy doing something — except one person.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Librum lego, magister. Fabulam de Roma lego.
lines.id: I'm reading a book, sir. A story about Rome.
lines.literal: book-obj read-I, teacher-call. story-obj about Rome-about read-I.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Bene. Et tu, Lydia? Quid facis?
lines.id: Good. And you, Lydia? What are you doing?
lines.literal: well. and you, Lydia-call? what make-you?

lines.speaker: Lydia:
lines.text: Epistulam scribo. Sed non bene audio — pueri clamant.
lines.id: I'm writing a letter. But I can't hear well — the boys are shouting.
lines.literal: letter-obj write-I. but not well hear-I — boy-pl shout-they.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Ita, pueri semper clamant. Quid vident?
lines.id: Yes, boys are always shouting. What are they looking at?
lines.literal: yes, boy-pl always shout-they. what see-they?

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: In horto Sextum vident. Sextus dormit!
lines.id: They can see Sextus in the garden. Sextus is asleep!
lines.literal: in garden-in Sextus-obj see-they. Sextus sleep-he!

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Dormit? In horto? Cur non venit?
lines.id: Asleep? In the garden? Why isn't he coming in?
lines.literal: sleep-he? in garden-in? why not come-he?

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: He's tired, sir. He's always asleep.

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Nos laboramus, Sextus dormit. Sic vita est!
lines.id: We work, Sextus sleeps. That's life!
lines.literal: we work-we, Sextus sleep-he. so life is-it!

lines.speaker: Lydia:
lines.id: Sir, what are you teaching today?

lines.speaker: Titus:
lines.text: Hodie de Graecia dicimus et fabulas antiquas audimus.
lines.id: Today we're talking about Greece and listening to ancient stories.
lines.literal: today about Greece-about speak-we and story-pl-obj ancient-pl-obj hear-we.

lines.speaker: Discipuli:
lines.id: We're listening, sir! We always listen!

notes: **Quid agis? has two meanings at once.** Literally "what are you doing?", but as an everyday greeting it means "how are you?". The standard answers are *bene* ("well"), *optime* ("very well") or *male* ("not so good"). Titus uses it here in its literal sense.

**Lego, legis, legit — the linking vowel changes.** Third-group verbs use *-i-* in some forms and *-u-* in the "they" form: *legimus*, but *legunt*. It's the only group that doesn't stay loyal to one vowel, and it's also the group with the most members.

**Facio and audio differ by one letter, but they're still two groups.** *Audio, audire* belongs to the fourth group; *facio, facere* to the mixed third group. The difference shows in the second form: *audire* ends in *-ire*, *facere* in *-ere*. That's why the dictionary form always lists both.
**Sic vita est.** *Sic* means "so, thus". You've probably seen it in quotations reproduced with their mistakes intact, marked *[sic]* — meaning "that's really how it was written".

blocks.text: Every Latin verb belongs to one of four groups, and you can read the group straight from the second dictionary form — the one ending in *-re*. What decides is the letter right before that *-re*.

head: Group
Dictionary form
Its sign
Meaning
rows: -ere, but the first form ends in -io

blocks.text: Groups II and III both end in *-ere*, and the only difference is the length of the *e* — something that isn't written. So you need one more clue: look at the first form. Group II always ends in *-eo* (*video*, *habeo*, *doceo*); group III always ends in a plain *-o* (*mitto*, *lego*, *dico*).

blocks.title: A quick way to guess the group
items: First form ends in **-o** and second form in **-are** → group I. Example: *porto, portare*.
First form ends in **-eo** → group II. Example: *video, videre*; *habeo, habere*.
First form ends in **-o** and second form in **-ere** → group III. Example: *lego, legere*.
First form ends in **-io** and second form in **-ire** → group IV. Example: *audio, audire*.
First form ends in **-io** but second form in **-ere** → mixed group III. Example: *facio, facere*; *capio, capere*.

blocks.text: The person endings are the same in every group — *-o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt* — exactly the ones you learned in Unit 3. Only the linking vowel before the ending differs.
Read the table downward, not across. Group I stays loyal to *a*, group II to *e*, group IV to *i*. Only group III moves around: *i* in the middle, *u* in the last row.

This mixed group doesn't have many members, but they're all common words: *facio* (make), *capio* (take), *fugio* (flee), *iacio* (throw), *rapio* (snatch), *cupio* (want). Learn all six at once and you're done with it.
This list isn't for memorizing in one go. Read it once, then come back here every time you meet one of them in a dialogue.
